Configuration Reference

Every command the audio engine understands, written against the source of OmniAPO 1.0.1 — the build installed on this machine. Works offline; nothing on this page loads from the internet.

No section matches that filter.

What this is

OmniAPO is an Audio Processing Object: Windows loads it inside audiodg.exe and hands it every sample on its way to (or from) a device. There is no server to start and nothing to keep running — if the device is enabled in the Device Selector, the engine is already in the signal path.

Why the folder still says EqualizerAPO. OmniAPO is a private build of Equalizer APO, and it deliberately keeps the original install path (C:\Program Files\EqualizerAPO) and registry key. Peace, HeSuVi and other front-ends locate the engine through exactly those, so renaming them would leave every one of those tools unable to find it. The new name is the product; the old name is the plumbing.

Its entire behaviour comes from plain text files. You edit a file, save it, and the change is live within about a second: the engine watches the config directory and reloads on its own. No reboot, no restarting applications, no toggling the device.

Two ways to edit. The bundled Configuration Editor gives you a graphical view with a live frequency response, and it writes exactly the syntax on this page. Anything it can do, you can also type by hand in Notepad. Text wins for version control, comments and conditional blocks; the Editor wins for dialling an EQ curve by ear.

If you edit by hand, save as UTF-8. In Notepad that is the encoding called UTF-8 — not Unicode, which is UTF-16 and produces a file the engine cannot read. Since 1.0.0 a UTF-16 file is refused with a message in the log and in Check configuration rather than loading as nothing; a UTF-8 file with a byte-order mark is accepted.

Before the first big edit, copy your config directory somewhere safe. An empty or malformed file will not damage anything — the worst case is that processing stops and unparsable lines are logged — but a good backup turns "what did I change?" into a five-second question.

Where the files live

PathWhat it is
C:\Program Files\EqualizerAPO\config\The config directory. Everything the engine reads lives here.
config\config.txtThe root file. The engine always starts here.
config\*.txtYour own files, pulled in with Include:.
VSTPlugins\Default folder for relative plugin paths (VST2 and VST3).
Editor.exeConfiguration Editor.
DeviceSelector.exeChooses which endpoints the APO attaches to. Needs elevation.
Benchmark.exeOffline harness — runs your config against a file, no audio device involved.
HKLM\SOFTWARE\EqualizerAPOInstallPath and ConfigPath. Other tools discover the install through these.

Why config.txt may look almost empty. A common and healthy layout is a root file containing only Include: lines, one per tool or concern. That way a GUI which owns one file can rewrite it freely without touching anything else. If Peace or another front-end is installed, expect it to own its own file.

How a configuration is read

The engine reads the file top to bottom and builds a chain of filters in that order. Order is the whole model: a Preamp after a limiter does something different from a Preamp before it.

Line format

Command: parameters

One command per line. The command name is case-sensitive; everything after the colon is the parameter text for that command.

Comments
A line whose first non-blank character is # is ignored. So are blank lines.
Unknown commands
Skipped silently — nothing is logged. They do not stop the rest of the file, but a typo in a command name leaves no trace at all, so check spelling first when a line seems to be ignored.
Decimal marks
Most numeric commands accept a comma as well as a period, so configs written on a German locale keep working. Preamp: -3,5 dB is valid.

What happens on save

  1. The engine notices the change and re-reads config.txt from the top.
  2. Conditions (Device, Stage, If) are evaluated once, at load time, for the device being configured.
  3. A fresh filter chain is built and swapped in.

Because conditions are resolved at load time, each audio device ends up with its own chain built from the same files. A single set of files can serve headphones, speakers and a microphone without interfering.

Runtime state resets on reload. Anything a filter accumulated — delay lines, convolution tails, plugin internals — starts fresh. Saving during playback can produce a brief click. That is expected, not a fault.

Channel names

Wherever a command takes channels, these names are accepted (case-insensitive; the parser upper-cases them). You can always use a 1-based number instead, which is the only option for exotic layouts.

NameSpeakerNameSpeaker
LFront leftRLBack left
RFront rightRRBack right
CFront centreRCBack centre
LFESubwooferSLSide left
SUBAlias for LFESRSide right

Side/back are interchangeable when only one exists. If a layout has side channels but you wrote RL/RR, the engine falls back to SL/SR and vice versa. This is why 5.1 configs written for one machine usually just work on another.

Gain & equalisation

Preamp: <gain> dB

Applies a flat gain to every channel currently selected.

Preamp: -6 dB
Preamp: -3,5 dB   # comma is fine

The unit is optional here, unlike elsewhere. Preamp: -6 applies −6 dB just as Preamp: -6 dB does — the value is read first and the dB that follows is not required. Write it anyway for consistency with every other command, but a missing unit is not what is wrong if a Preamp line misbehaves. Only a line with no readable number at all is rejected, and that is reported.

Always leave headroom. Any positive EQ gain can push a signal past full scale, where it clips hard. The rule of thumb is one Preamp near the top of the chain, set to the negative of your largest boost. Boost +6 dB anywhere, start with Preamp: -6 dB.

Filter: ON <type> Fc <f> Hz [Gain <g> dB] [Q <q> | BW Oct <b> | <s> dB]

One biquad section — the workhorse. The command may carry a trailing number (Filter 1:, Filter 2:) so exported files stay readable; the number is decorative and is not used for ordering.

TypeDoesGainWidth
PK PEQ ModalPeaking / parametric bellrequiredrequired
LS LSCLow shelfrequiredoptional
HS HSCHigh shelfrequiredoptional
LP LPQLow passignoredoptional
HP HPQHigh passignoredoptional
BPBand passignoredoptional
NONotchignoredoptional
APAll pass (phase only)ignoredrequired
NoneDisabled row — accepted and skipped silently——
Filter: ON PK Fc 1000 Hz Gain -4 dB Q 1.41
Filter: ON LS Fc 120 Hz Gain 3 dB
Filter: ON HP Fc 30 Hz
Filter: ON PK Fc 3150 Hz Gain -2.5 dB BW Oct 0.5
Filter: ON None

Width, three ways

Only one takes effect; the last recognised form on the line wins.

Q <number>
Classic quality factor. Higher is narrower.
BW Oct <number>
Bandwidth in octaves. Ignored for shelves.
<number> dB
Shelf slope, at the very start of the parameter text. Shelves only; internally divided by 12, so 12 dB is the maximum slope.

Omitting the width is not an error — it picks a default. These are compiled in and worth knowing, because a filter you thought was neutral is not:

TypeDefault when no width is given
LP HP BPQ = 0.7071 (½√2, Butterworth)
LS HSS = 0.9/12 — matched to Room EQ Wizard
NOQ = 30 — deliberately very narrow
PK APnone — the line is rejected and logged

LS vs LSC is not cosmetic. The trailing C means Fc is the true corner frequency; without it, the frequency is interpreted as the shelf's centre (the half-gain point). The same numbers therefore give two different curves. Room EQ Wizard emits the C forms; keep whatever your measurement tool produced rather than converting by hand.

Cascade for steeper slopes. One biquad rolls off at 12 dB/octave. Two identical HP lines give 24 dB/octave, three give 36. For a proper Linkwitz-Riley 24 dB crossover, use two sections both at Q = 0.7071.

Filter: ON IIR Order <n> Coefficients <b0..bn a0..an>

Raw IIR section for coefficients produced elsewhere — a filter designer, MATLAB, your own script. Order must be at least 1, and you must supply exactly (order + 1) × 2 numbers: all b (feed-forward) first, then all a (feedback).

# order 2 -> 6 coefficients: b0 b1 b2 a0 a1 a2
Filter: ON IIR Order 2 Coefficients 0.998 -1.996 0.998 1.0 -1.996 0.996

A miscounted coefficient list is rejected with the expected and actual counts in the log. An unstable set is not rejected — the engine will happily run a filter that blows up. Verify stability before you route it to speakers, and keep the volume down the first time.

GraphicEQ: <freq> <gain>; <freq> <gain>; …

An arbitrary response curve given as frequency/gain points, realised with a 16384-tap FIR. This is what AutoEq and most headphone-correction projects export.

GraphicEQ: 25 -1.5; 40 -1.2; 63 -0.8; 100 0; 160 0.9; 250 1.4

The separators are decoration. The parser simply pulls every number out of the line and pairs them up — first is frequency, second is gain, and so on. Semicolons, commas and extra spaces are all equally fine. A dangling odd number at the end is dropped. Points are sorted by frequency for you, so they need not be in order.

One decimal-mark rule to know. Commas are converted to periods only if the line contains no period at all. Mixing the two styles on one line (25 -1.5; 40 -1,2) parses the comma as a separator, so -1 and 2 become two different numbers and the whole curve shifts. Pick one style per line.

A 16384-tap FIR is the most expensive thing in this reference. It is perfectly affordable on a modern desktop, but if you are stacking several of them on many devices, Benchmark.exe will tell you the real cost.

LoudnessCorrection: State <0|1> ReferenceLevel <dB> ReferenceOffset <dB> Attenuation <0..1>

Equal-loudness compensation: as you turn the volume down, bass and treble are lifted to keep the perceived balance, following the ISO 226 contours.

LoudnessCorrection: State 1 ReferenceLevel 80 ReferenceOffset 0 Attenuation 1.0
State
0 or 1 — off or on.
ReferenceLevel
Integer dB SPL at which your system is considered "flat". 80–85 is typical.
ReferenceOffset
Integer dB trim if your calibration differs from the assumption.
Attenuation
0.0–1.0: how much of the correction to apply. Accepts a comma decimal mark.

All four keys are required and each is validated against a strict pattern — ReferenceLevel 80.5 is not accepted (integers only). If any key fails, the whole filter is dropped.

Routing & time

Channel: <names>

Selects which channels the following commands apply to, until the next Channel: line. This is modal — it changes state rather than processing audio.

Channel: L R
Filter: ON PK Fc 2000 Hz Gain -3 dB Q 2   # fronts only

Channel: LFE
Filter: ON LP Fc 80 Hz                     # sub only

Channel: all
Preamp: -3 dB                                # everything again

It stays in effect. Forgetting to switch back to Channel: all is the single most common configuration mistake — the rest of the file silently applies to two channels. If a change "does nothing" on some content, look upward for a stray Channel: line.

Copy: <target>=<source> [<target>=<source> …]

A full mixing matrix: build each target channel from a weighted sum of sources. All assignments on one line happen simultaneously from the pre-Copy signal, so swapping channels needs no temporary.

Copy: L=R R=L                       # swap, no temp needed
Copy: C=0.5*L+0.5*R                 # derive a centre
Copy: L=L+-3dB*R                    # mix in R at -3 dB
Copy: RL=0 RR=0                     # mute the rears
Plain factor
0.5*L — a linear multiplier.
Decibel factor
A factor ending in dB: -3dB*R.
Silence
0 on its own.

A bare whole number is read as a channel, not a gain. The rule is literal: a lone token counts as a factor only if it is exactly 0 or contains a period. So Copy: L=2 means "take channel 2", not "double L". Write Copy: L=2.0*L when you mean gain.

Targets beyond the current channel count are created on demand, which is how upmixing works. Remember that summing two correlated channels at full scale adds up to 6 dB — leave headroom.

Delay: <amount> ms | <amount> samples

Delays the selected channels. Combine with Channel: to time-align drivers or to compensate a subwoofer's position.

Channel: LFE
Delay: 6 ms
Channel: all
Delay: 128 samples

The unit is mandatory and only ms or samples are recognised. A negative value, or any other unit, is silently ignored — the line does nothing at all. There is no way to advance a channel; delay the other channels instead.

Roughly 2.9 ms per metre of air, so 1 ms ≈ 34 cm of speaker distance.

Convolution: <impulse-response file>

Convolves with an impulse response — room correction, headphone HRTFs, speaker cabinets, reverb. Any format libsndfile reads works (WAV, FLAC, AIFF…).

Convolution: room-correction.wav
Convolution: C:\IRs\hall.wav

Relative paths resolve against the folder of the file containing the line — not the config root. A Convolution: inside config\HeSuVi\hesuvi.txt looks in config\HeSuVi\. This is what lets preset packs ship as a self-contained folder.

The IR's channel count decides the behaviour: mono applies the same response everywhere, and a matching multi-channel IR applies per-channel responses. True stereo/binaural sets use a 4-channel IR. Sample rate is converted if needed, but an IR recorded at your device's rate avoids that step.

Plugins

VST3Plugin: Library <path> [CID <guid> | ClassIndex <n>] [ChunkData "<base64>"] [#<id> <value> …] This build

Hosts a VST3 effect inside the audio chain. This command does not exist in stock Equalizer APO — it was added in this build, alongside the older VST2 support.

# simplest case: a plugin with one effect class
VST3Plugin: Library LoudMax.vst3

# pick one effect out of a multi-effect module, and restore its state
VST3Plugin: Library "C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3\Airwindows Consolidated.vst3" \
             CID {B2C1F0A4-1234-5678-9ABC-DEF012345678} ChunkData "EAPOVST3STATE2..."
Library
Required. A .vst3 file or bundle folder. Relative paths resolve against <InstallPath>\VSTPlugins. Quote paths containing spaces.
CID
The effect class GUID, {XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX}. Prefer this for any module with more than one effect.
ClassIndex
Positional fallback. Works, but silently points at a different effect if the vendor reorders classes in an update.
ChunkData
Base64 state written by the Editor — component state, controller state and parameters in one envelope.
#<id> <value>
One normalised parameter (0.0–1.0) by numeric id. Repeatable.

Let the Editor write these lines. It enumerates the effect classes inside a module, shows the plugin's own interface, and emits the correct CID plus a ChunkData blob. Getting a GUID and a base64 state right by hand is not a good use of an evening.

Latency is compensated automatically. The host reads the plugin's reported latency and inserts matching delay on the untouched channels. One boundary worth knowing: if a plugin changes its latency while running — LoudMax's ISP switch moves 55 → 61 samples — the new value is picked up at the next config reload, not mid-stream. Re-save the file after toggling such an option.

A crashing plugin will not take your audio down. Plugin calls run inside structured-exception guards, and a plugin that faults is disabled rather than allowed to kill audiodg.exe. This is a safety net, not a licence to run unstable plugins — test new ones at low volume.

Unrecognised keys are reported in the log and skipped; the engine never guesses at what you meant.

VSTPlugin: Library <path> [ChunkData "<base64>"] [<name> <value> …]

The original VST2 host, unchanged. Relative paths resolve against the default plugin folder.

VSTPlugin: Library "Some Plugin.dll" ChunkData "..."

Prefer VST3Plugin for anything available in both formats: the VST2 SDK has been withdrawn by Steinberg, and VST3 is where plugin development actually happens now.

Conditions & structure

Device: <pattern>[; <pattern> …] Improved

Everything after this line applies only when the device being configured matches. Semicolons separate alternatives; Device: all re-enables everything.

Device: Speakers Realtek
Preamp: -4 dB

Device: Headphones; Kopfhörer          # either alternative matches
Convolution: hrtf.wav

Device: all
Filter: ON HP Fc 20 Hz

Within one alternative, every word must appear in the device's description (connection name, device name and endpoint GUID concatenated). Matching is case-insensitive and word order does not matter.

Changed in this build — renaming a device no longer breaks your config. Previously an alternative had to match every word and the GUID, so renaming a device in Windows Sound settings silently disabled the whole block. Now, if an alternative contains an endpoint GUID and that GUID matches, the alternative matches — the name words are no longer required. Patterns without a GUID behave exactly as before, and nothing that used to match can now fail.

Get the exact string from the Configuration Editor's device dropdown, which writes the canonical form Device: <connection> <name> {guid}. Because of the change above, that line is now rename-proof — it is the form worth standardising on.

Stage: pre-mix | post-mix | capture

Restricts the following lines to one point in the Windows audio pipeline. Several stages may be listed on one line.

pre-mix
Per-application, before Windows mixes streams together. Use it to treat one app differently.
post-mix
After the mix, on the final device stream. This is where most EQ belongs.
capture
Recording devices — microphones, line inputs, loopback.
Stage: capture
Filter: ON HP Fc 80 Hz        # rumble filter on the mic

Stage: post-mix
Preamp: -3 dB

With no Stage line, lines apply to capture devices, to post-mix, and to pre-mix only when no post-mix APO is installed — so a plain config is not silently applied twice on playback devices.

If: <expr>  ElseIf:  Else:  EndIf:

Conditional blocks, evaluated once at load time. Nesting is allowed.

If: outputChannelCount >= 6
  Copy: C=0.5*L+0.5*R
ElseIf: outputChannelCount == 2
  Preamp: -2 dB
Else:
  Preamp: 0 dB
EndIf:

Else: and EndIf: keep their colons — they are commands like any other, just without parameters. Omitting the colon makes them unknown commands that are skipped, which leaves the block open and produces very confusing results.

Eval: <expression>

Evaluates an expression for its side effect — typically defining a variable that later lines reuse.

Eval: nyquist = sampleRate / 2
Eval: house = readRegDWORD("HKCU\\Software\\MyTools", "HouseCurve")

Include: <file>

Reads another file at this point, as if pasted inline.

Include: peace.txt
Include: HeSuVi\hesuvi.txt
Include: presets\night-mode.txt

Relative paths resolve against the including file's own folder, so nested include trees stay portable. Recursion is capped at 100 levels; beyond that the include is skipped and logged, which makes an accidental include loop annoying rather than fatal.

The best structural habit in this whole reference: give every tool and every concern its own file, and keep config.txt as nothing but Include: lines. Switching presets becomes a one-line edit, and a GUI that rewrites its own file can never clobber your handwritten work.

Expression language

If: and Eval: use muParserX. Alongside the usual arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, these are predefined:

NameTypeMeaning
inputChannelCountintChannels entering the chain
outputChannelCountintChannels leaving it
sampleRatefloatDevice sample rate in Hz
stagestring"pre-mix", "post-mix" or "capture"
deviceNamestringDevice name
connectionNamestringConnection/jack name
deviceGuidstringEndpoint GUID
FunctionReturns
readRegString(key, value)A registry string — drive config from another tool's settings
readRegDWORD(key, value)A registry DWORD
regexSearch(subject, pattern)Whether the pattern matches
regexReplace(subject, pattern, replacement)The substituted string
If: sampleRate >= 88200
  Preamp: -1 dB
EndIf:

If: regexSearch(deviceName, "(?i)HDMI")
  Preamp: -6 dB
EndIf:

stage, deviceName and friends make If: a strictly more powerful alternative to Device: and Stage: when you need partial matches, negation or case-insensitive regex.

What differs in this build

Compared with stock Equalizer APO, five things behave differently. Everything else — file format, command set, install paths, registry keys — is unchanged, so existing configs and front-ends keep working.

1. VST3 hosting new

The VST3Plugin: command, with class selection by GUID, state persistence, automatic latency compensation and crash containment. Written from scratch for this build.

2. Renaming a device no longer breaks its config fixed

A Device: alternative carrying a matching endpoint GUID now matches regardless of the name words.

3. Disabling effects no longer silences capture devices fixed

With an empty filter chain and mismatched input/output channel counts — ordinary on microphones — the output buffer was never written, so the device went silent until Windows audio enhancements were toggled. Writing an empty config as a deliberate "off" state is now safe everywhere.

4. Illegal characters in device names are handled fixed

Devices whose names contain characters Windows disallows in filenames no longer break per-device file handling.

5. The engine repairs its own registration new

Windows feature updates occasionally wipe the APO registration on an endpoint, which silently disables all processing — audio keeps playing, your config simply stops applying. This build detects that at logon and in the Editor, and offers a one-click repair that runs elevated through the Device Selector. It asks first and never repairs silently.

Removed or unplugged hardware is deliberately not reported — otherwise every disconnected headset would produce a false alarm.

The build is also compiled for AVX2 with 64-bit double-precision processing throughout.

Recipes

A headphone correction that stays clean

# AutoEq-style curve plus deliberate headroom
Preamp: -6.5 dB
GraphicEQ: 21 3.5; 36 2.1; 63 0.4; 100 0; 1000 0; 5000 -2.3

Late-night listening

# tame the extremes, keep dialogue forward
Preamp: -3 dB
Filter: ON LS Fc 100 Hz Gain -6 dB
Filter: ON PK Fc 2500 Hz Gain 2 dB Q 1
Filter: ON HS Fc 8000 Hz Gain -3 dB

Save that as config\night.txt and switch with a single Include: line.

Microphone chain

Stage: capture
Filter: ON HP Fc 85 Hz                    # desk rumble, plosives
Filter: ON PK Fc 250 Hz Gain -3 dB Q 1.2  # boxiness
Filter: ON HS Fc 7000 Hz Gain 2 dB       # a little air
Stage: post-mix

Per-device split in one file

Device: Speakers {c1e4a8f2-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}
Include: speakers.txt

Device: Headphones {9b2f77d1-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}
Include: headphones.txt

Device: all

Safety limiter at the very end

# last line of config.txt, after every Include
VST3Plugin: Library LoudMax.vst3

Placed last, it catches whatever any earlier stage — including a front-end you do not control — leaves on the bus.

Hints & tricks

Work out loud in comments

Future-you will not remember why that -2.5 dB at 3.15 kHz exists. One # line per decision costs nothing and turns a config into something you can actually revisit.

Bisect a config that misbehaves

Comment out the bottom half, save, listen. The reload is instantaneous, which makes binary search the fastest debugging tool available here — usually quicker than reasoning about it.

Keep an A/B pair

Include: variant-a.txt
#Include: variant-b.txt

Moving one # switches the whole setup. Far more reliable than judging a change from memory.

Measure instead of guessing

Benchmark.exe runs your configuration against a file with no audio device involved. It answers "is this affordable?" and "what does this actually do to the signal?" without touching your listening setup, and it can process a WAV offline so you can compare before and after in an editor.

Prefer many small files

One file per concern — eq.txt, room.txt, mic.txt — assembled by config.txt. It keeps diffs readable and lets you disable one concern without unpicking a wall of filters.

Watch out for double correction

If a headphone DSP, a vendor "audio enhancement" and this config are all active, you are correcting a correction. Turn the others off before tuning here.

Positive gain always costs headroom

Every boost brings clipping closer. Cutting elsewhere and raising the system volume gives the same balance with more margin, and it is the reason most published curves start with a negative Preamp.

Version your config directory

It is plain text. git init in the config folder gives real history and one-command recovery from an experiment that went wrong.

Let the Editor write the hard syntax

Device lines with GUIDs, VST3 CID values and ChunkData blobs are mechanical to generate and painful to type. Produce them in the Editor, then rearrange the file by hand if you prefer.

Troubleshooting

Nothing I change has any effect

  1. Confirm the device is enabled in the Device Selector — and that it is the device Windows is actually using, not another endpoint with a similar name.
  2. Open the Editor: if the APO registration was lost, it will say so and offer to repair it.
  3. Check for a Device: or Stage: line above your edit that excludes the current device.
  4. Check for an earlier Channel: line still narrowing the selection.
  5. Make sure you edited a file that is actually reached by an Include: chain from config.txt.

Audio is distorted or crackling

Almost always clipping from positive gain. Add or lower a Preamp until it stops. If it persists with a large Convolution or several GraphicEQ curves, measure the cost with Benchmark.exe.

One line seems to be ignored

Run the checker first — it prints the engine's own reason for every line it rejected, which otherwise only reaches a log file nobody opens:

Benchmark.exe --check

Add --config <folder> to check a configuration before copying it into place. It exits with code 1 if anything was reported, so it also works in a script.

Two things it cannot tell you, because the engine does not report them either: a misspelled command name is dropped silently, and a bare whole number in Copy: selects a channel instead of setting a gain. Check spelling first.

Otherwise check the units — Delay needs ms or samples and Fc needs Hz, and without them the line does nothing at all rather than something approximate. Preamp is the exception: its dB is optional.

My microphone went silent

The old bug behind this is fixed in this build (see item 3). If it still happens, toggle the device off and on in the Device Selector and check whether a Stage: capture block is doing something unintended.

A plugin does not load

  • It must be 64-bit. 32-bit plugins cannot load into a 64-bit host.
  • Quote the path if it contains spaces.
  • For a module with several effects, specify CID — without it you get the first class, which may not be the one you want.
  • Check the log: load failures are reported with a reason.

It worked yesterday and stopped after a Windows update

That is the exact case the self-repair feature exists for. Open the Editor; if the registration was wiped it will offer to restore it.

Starting over

An empty config.txt is a valid, fully bypassed configuration. Rename your files aside rather than deleting them, confirm clean audio, then add them back one Include: at a time.

Tools & logging

Configuration Editor
Graphical editing with a live response graph, device dropdown, VST2/VST3 browser with class selection and plugin interfaces, plus the registration health check.
Device Selector
Chooses which endpoints the APO attaches to, per stage. Requires elevation; changes take effect when the device is next opened.
Benchmark
Offline harness. Runs a configuration against audio with no device involved — the safe way to measure cost or verify behaviour. --devicename, --connectionname and --guid let you test Device: matching without owning the hardware.
Logging
Parse errors, ignored parameters, plugin load failures and filter construction all go to the log. When a line does not do what you expect, the log usually names the reason outright.
